title.title: The Correspondence of Esther Roberts Hunt Collins

msIdentifier.institution: Friends Historical Library of Swarthmore College

projectDesc.p: The correspondence of Quaker minister Esther Roberts Hunt Collins is stored at the Friends Historical Library of Swarthmore College. With the generous support of H. David and Joyce E. Hunt, Library staff scanned and transcribed these letters in 2024 and encoded the text in TEI.

div.p:
The time runs long since I have had a a letter from thee, & I know that thee has equal right to think that. I have hardly done my duty. But I have go to out of the habit of letter writing that I seem as if I did not know how to begin on what to write when I have begun. We continue to enjoy the billing of health. Our black boy has had has had been the dropsy this winter, which has been our greatest trouble. But Doctor Pennell has cured him I believe completed. I have enjoyed (for my own part) my health better than ever I did for the same span of time. I weigh 185 lb, which is six or eight pounds more than either Brother Elisha or Stacy weigh & better than 20 lb more than I weighed last spring when I was in in Jersey. So that getting married seems to agree with me well enough. But my dear Mary rather exceed me for she weighs has gained near 25 lb in weight
since she came here to live. She complains some of her weak back but continues to go about her business, though I suppose that she will not be able to do so two months longer.

We live at the upper end of Bridgeport (which thee perhaps has heard before). I get any breakfast in the morning before I go to the store I there short days I don’t often go home until night. Rhodas’ little boy learns his book at home this winter & is his mother’s chief company in the day time. We have a comfortable house as any in the place (if it is not as large) but large enough for our family & to have for our friends when they please to call on us, & stabling for their horses. & always have had plenty to feed them & their horses with. I sold my saddle horse (that I had in Jersey last spring) & our carriage to William Yeates Senior of Alexander so that one cow & a few fowls is all the stock that we winter. The price of all kinds of county produce is far above what it used to be (for instance) wheat sells for $1.50 rye, & corn, $1.80, & oats $.50, bushel hay 12 bales a ton. Fortunately coal is cheap enough (is 6 cents per bunch delivered), for we have had a long severe cold spell of weather. I estimated by far
the longest spell of sleighing that I ever seen for the roads have been good ever since the cold weather commenced.

I think that fat horses will be seen in Jersey next spring if they have continued shipping there in preparation to what has been done here (for my own part I have not been in one). We have had a great fuss here this winter about the great National Road. The Bridgeport people have been turning themselves to have it to come into that town before it crosses the rim which the commission have at length connected to & the President has confirmed. They have began to dig down the hill on the other side of the River in good earnest & expect to do the same on this as soon as winter breaks up. & proper to build a the Monongahela as well as a permanent one over the mouth of the Dunlap Creek before many years. Brother Stacy has concluded to go to farming in the spring. Brother Elisha is to stock the plan for him & his is to farm to the Shaws. His wife is anxious to live on a farm & he is much in the spirit of it. Farming has been much better business in this county than it was to us. Guthrie proposes to go down the river in the spring. Our connections are all well here. Sister Mary’s head has got quite well I believe. Emmor talks much of his good parents & Aunt Rachel. Tis needless to say how agreeable it would be to our fathers & them here next summer as well as Brother David & Sister Rachel.

closer.salute: Accept for they self & father & Brother & Sister, though abundant is my love & esteem in which my dear R joined, thy son
